questions.q: What is the critical limitation of tenant settings, according to Microsoft's own documentation?
options: They control what's offered in the UI, but they're not a security measure — they don't change a user's underlying permissions
They only apply to Premium capacity workspaces
They can only be configured by a Microsoft support engineer
They take effect instantly with no delay
questions.explain: Tenant settings control feature availability in the interface, but a user with read access to a semantic model can still query and persist data even if a related tenant setting like Export data is disabled.

questions.q: How long can a tenant setting change take to apply across the organization?
options: Up to 15 minutes
Up to 24 hours
Instantly, with zero delay
Up to one week
questions.explain: Microsoft's documentation notes it can take up to 15 minutes for a tenant setting change to take effect for everyone in the organization.

questions.q: What is the current (non-legacy) path to reach tenant settings?
options: Sign in to Fabric, select OneLake catalog, then Govern, then Configurations > Tenant settings
Open Power BI Desktop and select File > Options > Tenant Settings
Go directly to admin.microsoft.com and select Tenant Settings from the sidebar
Tenant settings can only be changed via PowerShell, never through a UI
questions.explain: The current path is Fabric > OneLake catalog > Govern > Configurations > Tenant settings; the legacy path (during regional rollout) is Settings gear > Admin portal > Tenant settings.

questions.q: A tenant setting is 'Enabled for the entire organization except specific security groups.' What does this configuration mean?
options: The feature is on by default for everyone, with named groups explicitly carved out as exceptions
The feature is off for everyone except the groups listed
The setting has no effect until a group is explicitly added
This state does not exist in Power BI tenant settings
questions.explain: This state opens the feature broadly (enabled for the entire organization) while excluding specific named groups as exceptions — the opposite of scoping a feature to only specific groups.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend 'enabled for specific security groups only' as a safer default for sensitive features like external sharing?
options: It's closed by default and only opens the feature to the people who specifically need it, rather than the whole org
It's the only state that can be changed later without admin permissions
It automatically applies row-level security to the feature
It's required by Microsoft for all tenant settings
questions.explain: Scoping a sensitive setting to specific security groups lets an organization pilot or limit a feature's exposure instead of defaulting to organization-wide access.
